compute.reported_as: The autoregressive Jastrow factor is not translationally invariant and no other symmetries are imposed so that the number of variational parameters increases very quickly with system size like N_param ~ 1/2 (N_p N_s)^2. [...] For SR the learning rate was eta = 0.2. Alternatively to SR we use the reinforcement loss [...] Using stochastic gradient descent, the gradients are estimated over a batch of M ~ 200-300 samples [...] Fig. 12 shows that the largest part of the computation time is due to the inference of samples on the Slater determinant [...] Figure 12: CPU time per 100 samples (in seconds) of the most important computational tasks with cooptimization of the Slater determinant.
compute.source: Sec. 2.6 'Optimization and simulation details'; Fig. 12 caption; Fig. 14 caption ('with Adam used as an optimizer, batchsize is 200 samples'); Table 1 caption ('best variational energies across five random seeds'), arXiv:2210.05871 (compute pass 2026-09-16)
compute.note: Blanket statements only. Parameter count never given as a number (scaling formula N_param ~ (N_p N_s)^2 / 2 and 'N_param ~ N^4' in the Outlook; not derived here). Samples left null because the per-batch count is stated as a range ('M ~ 200-300 samples') in Sec. 2.6 and as 'batchsize is 200 samples' only in the Fig. 14 caption (4x4 convergence runs with Adam). All timing figures (Figs. 6, 7, 11, 12) are 'CPU time in seconds', so the device is a CPU but no model, core count, wall-clock or total time is stated; the conclusion says the implementation 'is slower than other neural network VMC schemes such as e.g. Slater-Jastrow-RBM' and that memory for the network parameters 'limits the simulatable system sizes to around 10x10'. Implementation in PyTorch. Whether the Table 2-4 runs used SR or Adam is not stated per table.
